utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Thursday, 2nd of April, 2009. Good morning, first, to the accused, to all the Defence counsel, and all OTP representatives, and the people assisting us. I know you have four IC numbers for us, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The Prosecution has submitted its objections to the list of documents tendered by 2D and 3D via witness Andjelko Makar. These lists shall be given Exhibit numbers IC975 and 976 respectively. It has also submitted its objections to 2D documents tendered via Witness Mario Milos. This list shall be given Exhibit IC977, and 2D has submitted its list of documents tendered via Witness Dragutin Cehulic. This shall be given Exhibit IC978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We're going to have the witness brought in, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Please stand up for your solemn declaration. Please state your surname, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomislav Kresic. The 26th of August, 1950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a BA in Economics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm the deputy manager or, rather, an adviser to the manager at the Punta hotel in Neum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you had an opportunity to testify before a court of law regarding the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this going to be the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated. Some introductory words. I suppose Ms. Nozica has told you that already, but to be on the safe side I'll repeat it. She'll first ask questions of you on topics that you probably addressed with her during the proofing for this testimony. Ms. Nozica will no doubt show you three documents that we have received and you have received in the pink folder on your right-hand side. I believe your screen is not working. If it doesn't work, then look at the documents you have available to you. Oh, it's working. Very good. But even had the screen not been working, we could have had your testimony. Do endeavour to be concise in your answers. If you fail to understand a question, do not hesitate to tell us, sir. Ms. Nozica is going to ask you first a few questions. It may be that the other Defence teams have questions for you as well. And Madam Prosecutor, on your right-hand side, may also ask questions of you. The four Judges in front of you might have questions based on the documents as well. So this is what I wanted to convey to you so that your testimony can take place as best as possible for you and in the interests of justice. You may proceed, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, good afternoon -- good morning.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, one person at a time, no overlaps. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You completed your secondary education and a degree in Economics in Sarajevo, in 1975 in the case of the latter; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In 1980, you were working in Sarajevo, and then the same year you returned to Neum and you got a job in the Bregava enterprise?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You continued to work for this company until 1984?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As manager?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In 1984, you were appointed manager of the Sunce hotel in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And this hotel was part of an enterprise named Arpo?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just to make this perfectly clear, it was a socially-owned company in its entirety; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Rather, a state-owned company?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In 1988, you were appointed president of Neum Municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you remained in that position --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please ask the witness not to overlap and not to speak at the same time. Thank you. The interpreter didn't hear the witness's answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Until 1990, the first multi-party elections, democratic ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In 1990, you returned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could counsel please explain to the witness not to speak at the same time as counsel. The interpreters can't hear both at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please just make a pause between my question and your answer. They're having some problems with the transcript. Mr. Kresic, how long have you known Mr. Bruno Stojic for?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I've known Mr. Stojic since sometime late 1981 and 1982. There was a need in the Bregava company for a commercial manager to be appointed, and then Mr. Stojic responded to a public tender about that position, since he had a BA in Economics. I interviewed him twice or three times, and I gave him an idea of what the job was about and what we expected the person doing that job to do. Mr. Stojic left a very favourable impression on me and my colleagues. A proper procedure was initiated, and then we appointed Mr. Bruno Stojic as assistant commercial manager. He had acquired some degree of experience, while in his student days, working in Dubrovnik over the holiday season in a number of different commercial enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How long did Mr. Stojic continue to work in that position as commercial manager in the Bregava company?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I switched over to the Sunce Hotel in 1984, and Stojic remained until 1986/1987, I think, stayed on as commercial manager in the Bregava enterprise, and then he moved on to work with the public utilities company in Neum. Neum is a tourist hotspot, and we wanted to keep it as clean as possible and as pretty as possible. Mr. Stojic was showing every sign of a person who was exceptionally diligent and capable, so he was elected at a Municipal Council meeting unanimously and appointed manager of the public utilities company in Neum.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was Mr. Stojic volunteering in certain positions at the same time, anything that had to do with the development of tourism throughout the municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic was exceptionally active. In the public utilities company, which obviously had to do with tourism as well, because they made sure the water was clean and the town was pretty, everything to do with the holiday season. And then he was appointed to the tourist board of the Neum municipality, and I even think he became its secretary and remained in that position for what I believe were two or three years, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Based on your recollection, how long did Mr. Stojic stay in that position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slow down, please, Witness, because it's difficult for interpreters to interpret you. Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] I think it was sometime in 1991 that Mr. Stojic left for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What job, what position?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Assistant minister of Internal Affairs, the police. I don't know what it was called, officially, but I think that was the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know if any of Mr. Stojic's family remained behind in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojic's family remained in Neum throughout, his wife and his two and then three children.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, did you know exactly what duties Mr. Stojic performed after he stopped working for the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know specifically about his positions after that, but I think he was working in the defence sector. I'm not sure what it was called at the time, but I think it was called the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Based on your recollection, was that in the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was later on, the HZ-HB, when it was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Stojic did after the war?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, after the war Mr. Stojic was pursuing some private business. I think it had something to do with a bank, or banking, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, we're looking at this entire period of time from the beginning of the war to when you claim he started pursuing some private business. Throughout this period, how often would you see Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: When he left for Sarajevo, he would still sometimes return to Neum the occasional weekend, that sort of thing. We would have a cup of coffee together, that sort of thing, on Saturdays and Sundays, because he was being -- they were keeping him quite busy in Sarajevo, and also he was busy with his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Stojic had a role to play in a sports club or anything like that in this period after the war?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojic had a role to play in the Basketball Association of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was also one of the founding members, I think, and honorary presidents of the Brotnjo Citluk Basketball Club. It was to a large extent thanks to him that a sports hall was built in Citluk, the Brotnjo basketball Club, and they only have him to thank for it; and the players, of course, became champions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they even took part in some European competitions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, were you friends with Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you friends with him family, and I mean his next of kin?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: When he came to Neum, there was a year of what I would term purgatory, in the sense that he was being tested continually. Well, how did he perform, what sort of a person was he? And then at one point, we ended up in exactly the same wavelength, and we became exceptionally close friends. Neum being an exceptionally small town, our family socialised as well, and we were very much on visiting terms, frequent ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know Bruno Stojic's family?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber who Bruno Stojic's family are?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: His wife and three children, to begin with. Two of the children have now obtained their BAs. The youngest one, Balavina, is now in secondary school. Furthermore, I know his parents very well; his father, Mirko, and mother, Paulina. I also know his brothers and his sister, but to a lesser extent. I do have to take this opportunity to say that Mr. Stojic's parents are exceptionally hardworking and honest people. They built everything with their own hands and through their own work, and thanks to the efforts of their father, Mirko, who came from the country-side; but then 40 or 50 years ago, given what the circumstances were, he was definitely showing signing of managerial acumen of the more rural type. That's where it all started, and all his children, and his son, Bruno, [Realtime transcript read in error, "Kruno"] in particular, I believe, had this sort of managerial talent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I may just observe line 21, instead of "Kruno," it should be "Bruno" because that is what the witness said. Mr. Kresic, you were close friends with Mr. Stojic. That is what you have suggested. In your opinion, what sort of a son, father, or spouse was Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I don't know about him as a spouse. Probably his wife would be best placed to tell you about that. Based on what I could tell, he was a very good husband and a very good father. I do have to throw in the occasional joke every now and again because we all somehow seem very serious here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That happens to be the procedure here in this courtroom, Mr. Kresic, but thank you anyway.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Let me just add something about his parents. Mr. Stojic had a BA and he was a manager, but he never hesitated for a moment, when he was required over in the country-side, his father's place, to help him prune the vines, and they had plenty of those, I can tell you that; dig up the soil, freshen up the soil, cut the new vines when the time came; and then eventually go there and pick the grapes every autumn, take those grapes, turn it into wine and brandy, so that every time he came back from the country-side, his arms and his back would ache, which means that he enjoyed working there and he enjoyed helping them; and obviously they, in their turn, enjoyed helping him whenever they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, do you know about the ethnic make-up of the employees in the public utilities company and headed by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the ethnic make-up was in that company or any other in Neum. This wasn't something that people kept track of, really. One thing that I can say: Back in 1981, I was head of the Census Committee, the Central Census Board for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Neum, as a municipality, was made up 95 percent of Croats, 2 or 3 percent Serbs, and 2 or 3 percent Muslims, and about 1 percent everyone else. As for the ethnic make-up of employees in various companies around Neum, and this was not something that people were really spending much time thinking about, I would conduct a census and then obviously I would have to go and ask; but we didn't really keep track of that sort of thing, but I think all three groups were represented in Mr. Bruno Stojic's company.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct of your last answer, all three ethnic groups were represented. What exactly do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: In addition to the Croats who were there, Mr. Stojic kept some Muslims and Serbs and Yugoslavs in his company, Yugoslavs being actually the fourth group.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You were municipality president for a while when Mr. Stojic was manager of the public utilities company. Do you know anything about Mr. Stojic's relationship with his employees, how he treated them, the employees in that public utilities company?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic was quite a severe manager. Nevertheless, his employees held him in high esteem, and I can even say he was well liked. He always found words of comfort or anything else that was required whenever an employee needed assistance, privately or in the line of duty. In addition to that, obviously it did no great harm that the salaries were decent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you ever observe Mr. Stojic draw any sort of distinction along ethnic lines among his employees, discriminating against anyone based on their ethnicity, or anything like that at all?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Not only did he never do that, what's more he even favoured a number of people. I know that for sure. The only group that was not enjoying his favours was those who were shunning work. At the time, nobody was counting blood cells exactly in terms of who belonged to which ethnicity. It was more about how you performed and what sort of person you were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said he was a severe manager. Can you tell us if there was any sort of referendum or an election held to appoint a manager among the workers at the time in the public utilities company? Is there anything that you can remember about that, in terms of Mr. Stojic being re-elected, and how did the employees take a vote?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Rumours went 'round Neum to the effect that certain managers did not deserve to have their term of office extended or that they were not good enough, and this made Mr. Stojic have a referendum, voting in his company. And I think he was voted in by as many as 96 percent of the employees. They voted in his favour, and that put an end to all the rumours going 'round Neum.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying that he was severe and strict as a manager?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: This means that instead of coming to work at 7.00 a.m., he would tour Neum at 6.00 a.m. to see if there was anything wrong, and then he would be at work at a quarter to 7.00 and watch when employees were coming to work. If anyone was late, he would get a telling-off from him. People couldn't leave work until working hours were over. And as this is a special sort of activity, for example, a pipe would burst in the plumbing or in the sewage, anyone who was in charge of that would have to come in even in the afternoon to repair the damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So he demanded discipline and hard work?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In his private life, did Mr. Stojic have friends of all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, in Neum, we were a multi-ethnic community, and many visitors arrived of all ethnicities. Through our work, we had close ties to Mostar, which was the regional centre, and to Sarajevo, which was the republican centre. I can say that some of Mr. Stojic's best friends were Muslims and Serbs, and even Jews, although there were few Jews, and so that's why I say "even Jews." I would like to support this by the fact that Mr. Stojic's best friend was Mirza. I think his last name was Smajlovic. He was the director of the Vodopriveda company, the waterworks company of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they had business associations as well, business links; and also with Mr. Bozo Knezevic, who is a Serb, again through the water utilities and waterworks affairs they were in charge of. He was also on good terms with Mr. Papo [phoen], who was the director of the roads of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because that also had to do with the infrastructure and utilities; not to mention lower-ranking people from Afan Sose [phoen] onwards, all of those who were working in those services. So I can confirm that he respected those people, he held them in high esteem, and they held him in high esteem. It was a mutual feeling.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just mention the following. He was also on extremely good terms with the then mayor of Tuzla municipality, Mr. Mirza Muratbegovic; and the director of the then salt factory in Tuzla, Safet -- his last name escapes me. And both these men are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, do you know whether Mr. Bruno Stojic was politically active when the multi-party elections started, so starting from 1991?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic always showed more interest in the economy than politics. Before the war, he wasn't very active, just a little bit in passing; but during the war, I don't think he was very prominent in politics. And after the war, I think there was an attempt, together with Mr. Kresimir Zubak, to found a party called the New Croatian Initiative as a sort of opposition party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that was -- well, this was not very successful. And then Mr. Stojic, I think, worked in a bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When did Mr. Stojic become active together with Mr. Zubak in a party called the New Croatian Initiative? What time-period was that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I think late 1997 or early 1998. It doesn't matter, but that's about the time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, can you tell Their Honours what you did during the war?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: In 1990, after the elections, I returned to the Sunce Hotel or the Sun Hotel as its manager, and I remained at that post until this year, practically. In the meantime, war broke out, and in the hotel we did work concerning logistics, putting up refugees and displaced persons, students, the wounded, convalescents, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say that you were a logisticians man, you said you were working for refugees, convalescents and so on, did you have any contact with the army and military units?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was for a while, as a hotel-keeper, the main logistics man, but that's as regards food, clothing, gas, water, batteries, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there an HVO unit based in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: In Neum, I think it was first a company and then it was a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What brigade did the battalion in Neum belong to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 1st Brigade, which was called the Knez Domagoj Brigade. It was established subsequently. It wasn't there from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And where was the Knez Domagoj Brigade stationed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I think it was around Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned refugees, Witness. When did refugees begin arriving in Neum, and where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: The first refugees to arrive in Neum arrived in August or September 1991, I think it was 1991, and they came from Stolac. They stayed for a short period of time and then went back there. After that, when there was an attack on Ravno municipality, the entire area of Ravno municipality and the Dubrovnik area from Slano to Neum, all the refugees from there arrived in Neum.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say they came from Stolac, was it just refugees of Croat ethnicity who arrived or were they people of all the ethnicities living in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, one should know that the area between Stolac and Neum is inhabited mostly by Croats, so there were the most Croats among them, but there were also Muslims and Serbs. I can give you specific examples. In my hotel, for a certain period of time, Mr. Mahmutcehajic resided. He was the father of the minister. I think his name was Irfan Mahmutcehajic. He was a minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so he stayed in our hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For how long did he stay in your hotel?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time we didn't keep those records. People stayed in the hotel for as long as they needed to, until someone -- some of their relatives arrived and took them somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question was whether they left voluntarily and whether they were able to stay in Neum for as long as they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: They could stay for as long as they wanted to, but all those who had relatives somewhere else went to stay with their relatives, they moved on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And did the same happen with Croat refugees? Did some Croats leave and others stay behind?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the entire Croatian population of the Dubrovnik Primorje area, after an intervention by the Dubrovnik authorities or Metkovic municipality - I'm not sure who - went to other accommodation in Croatia, so that the only people who remained in Neum were those who had nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Mahmutcehajic, and you said that his son was a minister in the Bosnia-Herzegovina government. Do you know that he had a son who was the logistics man of the 4th Corps of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I don't know that son of his personally. Since I was not involved in those military units, I didn't meet him, but I did know about that son of his. I think his name was Alija.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, you also mentioned convalescents. Can you tell to Their Honours who those persons were and how they were accommodated in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: After a certain period of time, after the war had been going on for a while, there were people who were sick, there were people who were wounded, and of course the wounded went to hospitals, from Metkovic to Split. Some of them were in hospital in Mostar. And after their hospital treatment, they would be sent -- I don't know who sent them, who referred them, but based on some referrals they would arrive in Neum, escorted by their wife or someone else, to take a rest. They no longer needed medical treatment, but they needed a rest. They needed to go to the seaside for the climate. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And were these people members of the HVO, the people you're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: They were members of the HVO, yes, but I think that at the time there were people of other ethnicities in the HVO, not just Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we take a look at a document, and then we'll come back to this issue. The document is in your binder. It's 2D972. It's -- well, this binder is not in consecutive order, but there are only three documents in it, so it should be easy to find. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a decision signed by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, and the date is the 27th of August, 1992. And it says that all wounded members of the HVO can use a ten-day vacation at the Sunce Hotel in Neum based on a suggestion by the command of municipal headquarters in their brigades, and it says that this can begin from the 1st of September, 1992. So, Mr. Kresic, when you spoke about members of the HVO of all ethnicities, as you said, who stayed in the hotel in Neum for rehabilitation or for a rest, as you say, is this a document which confirms what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, I hadn't seen this document before because it's not addressed to me, but based on a decision made by somebody somewhere, we received these convalescents with their escorts, with their companions, and most of them stayed in the Sunce Hotel and some of them stayed in another hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you again whether you knew that these were people who were members of the HVO and that they were of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, all I know for certain is at that time in the HVO, there were members of all ethnicities, although later on there weren't many. But in this period, there were quite a few. After the war, a good number of Muslims remained on the, let's say, left bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd now like to go back to the issue of the functioning of the authorities in Neum. Can you explain to Their Honours how the local government functioned, how it was focused, where it was concentrated?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, I have my opinion about this. I'm not familiar with the details, but I think that authority was concentrated in the hands of the mayors or the presidents of the municipalities, not just in Neum but in every municipality, and their circle of close associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, as regards Neum specifically, who was the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality in Neum was Mr. Ivan Bender.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As you say, you did some logistics work for the army. Do you know how the army was financed in Neum municipality in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know something about this, although I'm not quite sure, but in 1992 funds were paid to a municipal HVO bank account; and these funds were used to finance the general needs, including the salaries, the pay, of the members of the Neum company. Later on, when the Croat community was established, I think that was the way pay was handed out, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say that some funds were paid. Who paid those funds?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: The companies and enterprises in Neum. There was no pension fund, no social security fund, so these funds were contributions from people's salaries which were paid to that bank account, and this was used to finance the expenses of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say "when the Croatian community was established," do you mean the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know what the staffing policy was in the unit which was in Neum? Did they have regular contacts with the president of the municipality, and what was the relationship between the municipal authorities and the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Initially, the organisation worked very well, but when the fighting really started, everybody tried to avoid, as far as they could, these contacts. And then a nucleus was formed, and from that nucleus of HVO members and, of course, the people who were in the party, a leadership was formed, the leadership of the company which later grew into a battalion. Of course, they had meetings and consultations with the head of the municipality or the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the head of the municipality and the command of the company?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, the command. Well, they had meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can you just wait for me to finish putting my question before you reply. If I understood you correctly, the president of the municipality held regular meetings and consultations with the command of the company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, as you said, was the president of the municipality. Do you think what other posts he held in Neum, what other duties he performed? Was he the president of the HDZ in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: At one period of time, yes, he was. He was in the HDZ Presidency of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Bender was a member of the Presidency of the HZ-HB as the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, did you have any conflicts with Mr. Bender because of the fact that he held absolute power in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that we had different opinions about the problems in Neum and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, of course, I and some other people who had perhaps a different opinion were sidelined, passed by, attacked, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you arrested or brought in at some point?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993, on the 12th of May, in the morning at around 8.00 a.m., four uniformed men entered the hotel with long barrels and showed me a piece of paper, some sort of warrant. They waved it at me from some distance and told me I was under arrest and should go with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. It was said that people entered the hotel with long barrels. I wonder whether fire-weapon was long barrels was the meaning. Witness, did you say that the people who entered the hotel had guns with long barrels in contrary to short-barrelled pistols or revolvers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw them as cannons. To me, they appeared to be cannons, because when somebody turns up early in the morning -- they had weapons. I can't describe the weapons precisely, but they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, apart from you, were others brought in on that day in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Five of us were: The director of the utilities company, Mr. Rade Lasic; Mr. Nedeljko Babic, who was the director of the health centre; Ante Konjevoda, who was the director of the Neum Hotel; and Slavko Katic, the chief of the defence office --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Head of the defence office, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were pushed in a van and taken to the barracks in Capljina, to a room there, where we were put on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Why were you taken away, and where?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, I already said we were taken to the barracks in Capljina. And the reason we were taken there was so that individuals could demonstrate their power and intimidate other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When were you released?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: We were released that night at around 1.00 a.m. or 12.30, after midnight. We were in that room. We were brought some food for our supper, but we didn't feel like eating much. And then in the night, at around 12.30 or 1.00 a.m., a uniformed gentleman arrived and ordered that commander or deputy commander of the barracks to release us, and he then responded noisily. He cursed and swore and said he would not release us. He did, in fact, release us, but while we were getting ready he went on cursing, asking who had issued the order for us to be released and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say that this was done to demonstrate power and intimidate other people, what other people are you referring to? Are you referring to citizens of Neum or someone else?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, the citizens in general. We didn't obstruct anything, we had nothing to do with anything, but somebody needed an alibi or a reason, a scapegoat in fact. They wanted to find an excuse for their failures. Instead of admitting their failures and their lack of success in some activities, they blamed us for their failure in order to justify themselves before the military or civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: While you were detained, did you have contact with persons who were in charge of detention there? Did you have any conversations with anyone? Were you told why you were there? Were you given any information as to what was happening and why you were there?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: We had no information indicating why we had been brought there. After a couple of hours, we were told that we had been detained over military issues, regardless of the fact that we had nothing to do with any military issues. The gentleman who was the one talking to us, or perhaps it's better to say yelling at us, this man named Boko, Bosko Previsic, told us that we were not good men and that we were not good Croats, summing that up as the reason we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: During the interviews, did they do anything to place you in the same context with Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: When this man came to release us, I eventually realised that this had something to do with Bruno Stojic because we hadn't been talking to anyone at all during that day. Nevertheless, Mr. Boko was swearing and cursing Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic, and a number of other persons, too, that he had no regard for them, that they weren't proper authorities and he would not release us. There was an altercation. The man came to get us. He quarrelled with Boko and then we were released. He demeaned Stojic in such a way verbally that I think this must have had something to do with an issue that he had with Stojic, he or another person from his own group.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you ever find out who had issued the warrant for your release?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the warrant came from, but it must have been Mr. Stojic or someone working closely with him. Our wives had called everyone they knew. They had tried talking to everyone they knew, but I think Stojic was probably the key man for our release.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now please look at 2D515. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: What was that number?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report on how a group of citizens from Neum were detained the 15th of May, 1993, drawn up by the Security Sector. Mr. Kresic, can you perhaps remember whether anyone from the Security Sector interviewed you at any point following your detention?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next day after I had returned from detention, I made an official request to the HB authorities for the matter to be looked into, as to who had ordered our arrest and for what reason. Two or three days later, Mr. Ivan Bandic arrived, and he was a member of the Security Service. He interviewed me as well as Mr. Slavko Katic, who was the head of the Defence Department in Neum.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was that the defence bureau or office?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now please go to page 2 of that document, the report, the one drawn up by Mr. Bandic. This is 2D0390076 in the English, 2D0390076. That's the English reference. Paragraph 3 from the bottom of the page up. This is exactly what it says, what you say Boko Previsic said: That a military policeman had called, a person who introduced himself, to order their release. The person introduced himself as Minister Stojic. He made that request, and then Previsic responded that he refused to acknowledge a minister who allowed his soldiers to be captured at Konjic. Are these the allegations made by Boko Previsic while you were there in detention?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: This is only a record that was drawn up, and obviously a bit of a milder spin or spit on Mr. Previsic's words, compared to the way they were actually uttered.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We only have a very short time left and two rather brief subjects to go through. Therefore -- I do apologise. I think we'll have to go back to this document. Page 2, please. Page 2, there's a reference there to Mr. Ramljak who was also in that prison, the previous page says talking to Jelko, the prison warden. We found out that the group had been brought into prison at five minutes past 12.00. In addition to that, Ramljak said that at about 1.00 on the 12th of May, he was informed over the phone by his deputy, Boko, that the prison had been attacked and that they were trying to use force to get those detained on the previous day released. His deputy was in a panic and obviously nervous. He tried to calm him down and see what the whole thing was about. Immediately after that, Ramljak phoned Dragan Curcic, or at least that's how he introduced himself, as Ramljak says, who was swearing, yelling, and making threats to the effect that those people should be released, that he had received order from Boban to that effect, and so on and so forth. Ramljak responded by saying that he had no power to have anyone released because the detention order had been passed by the Knez Domagoj Brigade and that the other man should now try and get in touch with Obradovic. Mr. Ramljak says that he then proceeded to get in touch with Mr. Obradovic, or at least made an attempt to do that, get in touch with Obradovic and [indiscernible], but he was unable to locate them. And the warrant for their release was produced by Milenko Manala [phoen], Obradovic's deputy, after which those people were released. Sir, can you remember, learning about this, that it was at the request of Obradovic and the Knez Domagoj Brigade that you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I may have heard something to that effect later on. People were talking about this. But at the time, we knew nothing. We were brought in and put out of sight.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This document even claims that there had been an order by Mr. Boban. Obviously, nevertheless, it was said at the time that not even his order was sufficient for your release without Mr. Obradovic's approval. Do you remember things like that being said at the time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: The main culprit for us being detained was the group of people from Neum and Capljina. Was Obradovic involved or anyone else, I can hardly say. I have no information on that. The fact remains Obradovic had to know about this, and so did Markovic and Bender. They all knew. As for the conversation between Ramljak and Boko Previsic, I think Ramljak said Boko sounded somewhat timid on the phone when he was talking to him, but that was Boko's normal tone of voice, that's what he usually sounded like. Boko was very much minded to keep us there, but he had to give in eventually. The man came with someone's warrant, following which we were released, and in all this din and noise he eventually released us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's try and wrap this up, Mr. Kresic. What is your final opinion on this? Were you detained because you were actively opposing Mr. Bender and the people surrounding him? Briefly, please. I do have other questions to ask you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, I was detained simply because my opinion was different from theirs. And I would say my opinion was normal, unlike theirs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there any ban on entering Neum at the time? Was anything like that in force, barricades or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was very outset of the fighting in the surrounding areas, obstacles were placed in the way into Neum, and these obstacles or check-points were manned. At first, they weren't wearing uniforms. Then they sort of wore semi-uniforms, and then uniforms. And they were checking everyone on their way into Neum.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were they issuing permits and were they in charge of determining how long a person would be allowed to stay in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I think they were there to both allow and refuse entry, and also to determine how long a person would be allowed to stay in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were those persons members of the army or perhaps of the Neum Company, the one we talked about?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Those were people from Neum who were there to perform checks. It was some sort of a unit, military or something, and they were part of the general Neum security.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: 1992 and early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did an incident occur at the time, perhaps, in relation to Bruno Stojic's family, and they were still living in Neum, as you said, something to do with visiting and this permit being issued? Do you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I think the most --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom. I understand that Ms. Nozica is now going to get into an incident with regarding the Stojic family. We have no notice of this in summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you don't have any time left, so the time you're using now has to be taken out of the time remaining for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. This is part Mr. Kresic's general knowledge concerning Bruno Stojic's family. I have a very short question in relation to the last document and that's all that remains, so may I be allowed to use this time in order to then go on and complete?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask your question now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you answer, please, Mr. Kresic? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: There was this one situation that remains etched in my memory. When his wife gave birth to a baby, his sister and his son-in-law and were allowed in, but it took a full two hours of to and fro, a bit of a tug-of-war, and then they were eventually allowed to go and visit Bruno's wife. But they had overstayed the two hours they were allowed to stay there, and then the military police came and got them out of the Metkovic area. It was a mixture of tragedy and comedy, one might say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Eventually, 2D975, that's the last document that we'll be looking at. Mr. Kresic, do you know this man, Pero Kralj from Gradac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mr. Kralj from Gradac in the Neum area. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that before the war, he was working with the Atlantic Overseas Ship company before the war in Dubrovnik in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know whether he at one point lost his job or, rather, he received a decision terminating his contract with that company, which occurred sometime in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj lost his job. He was drinking coffee with me at the Sunce Hotel because that's where his wife was working at the time. He came there to drink coffee with me, and as soon as he came, he told me that he had lost his job.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If we look at the first document, the first page, we see that Mr. Kralj was informed by his company that under the employment law, he was not a national, he was a foreign citizen, and that he could only get another employment contract if he was permanently resident in the Republic of Croatia and if he had an actual work permit letter, and the decision says that failed to meet those conditions, for which reason his contract was terminated. And then there's a decision, and the decision is to be found on page 2 of this document. First of all, was Pero Kralj an ethnic Croat?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. If we look at this document, we can see that there were regulations in Croatia, to be sure enough, saying that foreign nationals would only be allowed to be gainfully employed if they met a set of very particular conditions. Mr. Kresic, you were the manager of the Sunce company. I'm only asking you because this goes back to the beginning of the war. Were you bound in any way under the law in relation to persons who failed to show up for work, who did not report to work? Were you supposed to fire them?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Our law says that if a person fails to show up for work for between five to seven days without any proper justification, their contract should be terminated. That is the sort of regulation that was applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina and I think the same was true throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about you -- at very outset of the war, there were people who were no longer coming to work. Did you at any point in time, under the provisions of this law, fire anyone?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: All those who failed to appear for between 10 and 15 days were eventually fired, be they Croats, Serbs, or Muslims. I have examples of all of these, but I was not alone in making these decisions because everyone else did the same thing in situations like these.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kresic, thank you, this concludes my examination. Your Honours, I'm now done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before the break, I have two brief questions for you. I understood that you were the president of the Neum Municipality and in 1990, and if I understand properly, you were then a member of the Communist Party so that you became the president of the municipality. Therefore, you were bound to know a lot of people, including Mr. Stojic and his family. How do you account for the fact that Mr. Stojic, who had obvious commercial skills because he was recruited to work in the hotel, how do you account for the fact that a few years later he became head of the Defence Department and later minister for Defence? Do you have any information accounting for this unusual career, somebody working in a hotel who finds himself later on a minister for Defence? This must be a rare occurrence in the world. Do you have an explanation for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I was not a member of the Communist Party. I was a member of the League of Communists. There's a difference there. It wasn't because of that that I was appointed municipal president. It was because of my knowledge, because of my ability, and I was appointed by the delegates of the then Municipal Council. Being a member of the League of Communists was not really key for becoming a manager or a municipal president. There were some people who occupied those posts who actually weren't members. As for Mr. Stojic, he was an exceptionally capable organiser. Now, this was a new, big challenge facing him, going to Sarajevo; but he had previously been manager of a public utilities company, not of a hotel, and now he suddenly became minister, the Interior minister, no less. This is quite a spectacular promotion and quite a spectacular challenge as well. When he left for Sarajevo, there was no war. The Croats and the Muslims were hoisting their flags together and were still keeping together. I think that was seen by Mr. Stojic as an enormous challenge. He wanted something more, and Neum was no longer large enough to satisfy his ambition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question: It is connected to the obscure reasons why you were arrested and detained for some time, later to be released. I did try to understand, but it seemed rather complicated, and I really don't have an answer. I have a lot of questions. One of the theories that I have that I'd like to put to you, in order to try to understand, is this: It appears that you were quite close to Mr. Stojic back then. Mr. Stojic was part of the HVO apparatus, because we know that he was the head of the Defence Department and then Defence minister. We also know that the Neum municipality was then headed by Ivan Bender and that this municipality could play a part at the level of the Presidency of the Croat Community. When you were arrested, could that not be explained by some kind of rivalry within the HVO apparatus and all these municipality leaders who would like to gain power? Were you perhaps the victim of some kind of a conflict, which might account for the fact that you were arrested, or do you have perhaps another explanation that might shed some light on the issue ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I've pointed out already, I believe that we were detained for one reason alone. They were trying to find an excuse for their own failures. They were trying to intimidate people. They reckoned if they were able to simply arrest four or five of the leading people in Neum and get away with it, and after all, these people were in leading positions, what then could an ordinary man expect? There was no need to prove anything else, because their power by now was absolute. At the time, Mr. Stojic most certainly had nothing to do with any military bodies, regardless of the fact that he was a minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that you were arrested because someone wanted to, as it were, mask their failures. As for Mr. Ivan Bender's failure, what was the duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just Ivan Bender. There were other people involved in this, in both civilian and military bodies. They probably had some plans. I didn't know their plans. I wasn't privy to their plans because I wasn't a member of their circle. Nevertheless, they were up to something, and they failed. Was it about setting up civilian authorities, military authorities? Whatever, but they needed a scapegoat, and they found us. They were suddenly faced with a great amount of resistance from many, many people in Neum, and they realised that their plan had no future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Before the break, does the 3D team have questions, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have a number of questions for this witness, Your Honour. A total of four minutes, I think, would do. I can start right away, if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kresic, I'm Vesna Alaburic, an attorney at law from Zagreb. I will ask you several questions on behalf of General Milivoj Petkovic, a number of additional clarifications in relation to issues regarding your arrest. If I understood correctly what you said, you were arrested, or at least that's what you were told, based on an order from the commander of the 1st HVO Brigade, Mr. Nedeljko Obradovic; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was told, but I never saw the actual order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, at the time of your arrest, you were a civilian or a military person?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, according to the regulations that were being applied throughout Herceg-Bosna, what about the commanders of brigades or any other HVO units; were they allowed to issue arrest warrants in relation to civilians?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We were civilians, despite which we were arrested. On whose orders, I don't know. There doesn't seem to be any paper trail that I'm aware of. That is why I asked to submit a report to someone from the Security Service. That was -- when Mr. Ivan Bandic came over, he listened to our story, and he drew up an account -- a record of it, rather, which I then received two months later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You say "which I then received two months later." You received it two months later; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on this, I assume, and this is new to me, that you were the one who had initiated this interview with the people from the SIS; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I wanted to have some sort of paper trail, if you like, documents to show for this, so that I myself knew what it was exactly and why we had been detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, as far as you know, following this incident was the commander of the HVO's 1st Brigade dismissed, or perhaps his SIS assistant, Zara Pavlovic, whose name is also mentioned in this document, or indeed was anyone else fired from the Knez Domagoj HVO 1st Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I was not a military man myself, nor indeed did I know about any dismissals, or removals, or replacements. I don't think anything actually happened. I think they just decided to gloss over it and go ahead with their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your information, was someone perhaps initiating anyone -- again, my question: Mr. Kresic, based on your information, was there any sort of procedure that was initiated for anyone's removal and then for some reason this came to nothing? Did you know anything about anything like that going on?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I simply wasn't involved in the work of those bodies, particularly military ones. I don't think anyone was eventually replaced, and I don't think anybody was called to account for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D?

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6D?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prlic Defence will have two issues to raise with this witness about subjects that were brought up during the chief, ten minutes maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have the break now, since it is 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. Kresic. I'm co-counsel for Mr. Jadranko Prlic, and I will put a few brief questions to you in connection with your testimony during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, you said that for many years you were and still are the manager of the Sunce Hotel, which was part of the Apro Corporation Holding Company; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of interpretation, please count to five before you respond to my question. We'll look at some documents right away. Please take the blue binder have you before you, and the first document you will find there is 1D03136. That is the longer document you see here. It is a prospectus containing a description of the activities of Apro Holding. Do you recognise the prospectus?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that I participated in writing this prospectus, so I am very familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the information of the Their Honours and the Prosecutor's office, I have the original of the prospectus here, if anyone would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at the page most interesting for us at this moment. In the bottom right-hand corner, you have numbers starting with "1D," and find page 1D580204. That's towards the end of the booklet.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: This book is in German and English. There is no Croatian translation, but I don't think that will be a problem. In addition to your company and your hotel, on this page we can see that Apro Holding also encompassed about 36 companies, 111 basic organisations, that it had 14.500 employees, and that about 6.000 farmers participated or, rather, were part of Apro Holding. This is information from 1983. Can we agree, then, that when the war broke out in 1991, this company was even bigger, far bigger than depicted in this prospectus?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your estimate as to how many employees were then employed in Apro Holding?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: We in Apro Holding had between 15.000 and 16.000 employees around 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you look through this prospectus, can we agree that Apro Holding also encompassed various types of companies; research institutes, service companies, manufacturing companies, and trading companies?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree also that the largest number of employees were actually employed in the manufacturing companies?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next document. It's already in evidence. That's 1D02390, and it's information on the situation in the Apro Corporation Mostar Holding Company, submitted to the HVO of Mostar Municipality, the Economics Department, on the 4th of June, 1992. This is information was delivered by the then general director, Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Please take a look at page 4 in your version, and for the Judges it's page 2. I'm interested in the paragraph that begins with the word "Ukratko," in your version, and for the Judges, "Shortly." It's the last item in paragraph 2, and I will read it to you.

utterances.speaker: DR. JADRANKO PRLIC SAYS
utterances.text: "In short, due to the war, almost all manufacturing activity has ceased, and the greatest damage is expected in perennial crops, (almost 3.500 hectares of vineyards and orchards). Detailed information on the damage will be obtained only after we have surveyed the situation, which is at present impossible, for understandable reasons." As you were there, you will agree that Dr. Jadranko Prlic, as the general director of Apro Holding, delivered to the HVO of Mostar Municipality correct information?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that most employees were employed in manufacturing companies, we may assume that these employees, in fact, lost their jobs or could no longer work for the simple reason that there was no work?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: In our Law on Labour Relations, the one that was in force before the war, when such a situation arose there was a legal provision stating that such workers would be put on standby; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: So we may conclude that the vast majority of employees were, in fact, on standby; they hadn't, in fact, lost their jobs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, I would put it differently. The vast majority of the workers were left without work because the areas in which they worked were devastated. Factories were destroyed, burnt down, they were inaccessible, and some of the employees were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the document I showed you previously, in this Apro Holding prospectus, we saw information on the number of employees in 1983, but nowhere in that prospectus can we find information as to the percentage of Muslims, the percentage of Croats, or the percentage of Serbs. Were records of this kept in Apro at all?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: We in Apro were only concerned with employing people who were professional and who wanted to work. There was also a social welfare element. In certain backward areas, work-places were opened up so that people would remain there; for example, in Duvno, Tomislavgrad, Nevesinje, Popovo Polje, and so on. But nobody cared about the ethnic make-up of the employees in any company, nor were any records of this kept at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: So based on everything we have said, we may conclude that the policy of Apro Holding in 1992 was not to fire all Muslim employees, but rather that the wartime situation brought the economy into such a state that people lost their jobs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: The idea that somebody wanted to fire employees of another ethnicity is not correct. A large proportion of Serbs and Muslims remained in what we can conditionally refer to as Croatian areas. I can give you quite a few examples of this. And in Neum, there were Serbs and Muslims who remained. The only ones who left were those who left of their own accord, of their free will. And regardless whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims, if they didn't show up for work for five to seven days, they were fired, in compliance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll now move on to another topic, and this topic concerns the functioning of the local government in Neum. In addition to being the managing director of Apro Holding at that time, and your managing director, Dr. Prlic was also a professor at Mostar University?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was, the university based in Neum.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: We heard testimony here that Mostar University was relocated to Neum in late 1992 because, for security reasons, it was impossible to organise classes in Mostar. You know that Dr. Prlic continued lecturing at Mostar University even then, do you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he travelled to Neum regularly in order to give those lecture?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him many times.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Prlic ever complain to you that when he arrived in Neum, the people -- the local people would allow him to stay in Neum for only two hours, and after two hours he would have to go back?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Well, those are those ridiculous situations when a professor arrives at a check-point and some guard tells him he can't pass through or that he can only stay for two hours, and then he has to go back. This means that at that time, Dr. Prlic found it more difficult to enter Neum than other professors did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that at the time, Dr. Prlic was not just a professor; he was also the president of the interim executive authorities, the interim executive board of the HVO. Did that change the situation at all?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: At that time, Prlic was not an important person in politics. His importance was very small in Herceg-Bosna, and it was nonexistent in Neum. He was seen as a man who was supposed to organise civilian life, civilian authorities, and linking up with the areas controlled by the HVO because that was where he had experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kresic. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just need a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Kim West. I'm with the Office of the Prosecution, and I'm just going to ask some follow-up questions. May we have P100608. It's a map, P10608. You have a binder next to you, the black -- the actual binder, and we're going to refer to a number of documents in there. Can you turn to P10068. This is a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P10068; and it's map 39. There you go. Sir, in front of you, you have a map of the entire BiH, and just so we have an idea of where Neum is located, can you just point out on the board -- you have in front of you a pen that you can use to mark on the board, and if I can have the usher's assistance, you can just circle where Neum is located.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: This is Neum here [marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So right next to the red dot that you put on the screen; correct? And can we have an IC number for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The map just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC00979. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, you had indicated in your direct testimony that in 1981, you were the head of the Census Committee. Would you agree with me that by 1991, the next census ten years later, there was an absolute majority of Croats living in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I said in 1981.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And my question is: Would you agree with me that by 1991, ten years later, there was still an absolute majority of Croats living in Neum?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: The ethnic make-up of the population in 1981 and 1991 was almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to P10912. This is another map, P10912. P10912. I'm sure you can see on the screen in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There you go, and it's the colour version in front of you. This is information on Neum from the actual 1991 census. And in 1991, do you agree with me that the total population of Neum municipality was 4.325 or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And of that number, the number of Croats was 3.792, the number of Serbs was 207, and the number of Muslims is 190, the number of Yugoslavs was 90, and the number of others and unidentified was 46. Does that appear accurate to you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in your testimony today, you actually indicated that in Neum, you were a multi-ethnic community. Would you agree with me that although there were at least four ethnicities in Neum, the primary ethnicity was Croat?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Kresic, from late 1992 to early 1994, was there any actual fighting going on in the municipality of Neum between the HVO and the ABiH, actual conflicts, battles going on?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: The conflicts between the BH Army and the HVO did not occur on the territory of Neum. The fighting that took place in Neum was between the Serbian Army, the Army of the SAO Krajina or whatever it was called, the Serbs, and our HVO, but there was no conflict with the Muslims in Neum.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you also agree that the ABiH didn't even have a presence in Neum during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't fully agree with that. Some members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were present in Neum. They had training there and exercises.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fair enough. So they were training there, but they weren't involved in any conflicts with either the Serbs or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: No, that he weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you had --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: On the territory of Neum, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. You described in your direct testimony sort of the government of Neum, and you indicated that Ivan Bender was in charge in Neum. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you agree with me that Ivan Bender was a founding member of the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: He was one of the founders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you would also agree that had the HVO been dissatisfied with his performance in Neum, they could have dismissed him?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: You mean remove Bender?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KRESIC
utterances.text: It wasn't easy to remove him. He was the authority there. He would hardly remove himself. Every municipality was an authority in itself, and the representatives of the municipalities made up a broader organisation. It wasn't easy to replace one. Bender never wanted to replace himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But the HVO municipalities -- or the government that Bender was in charge of in Neum was under the auspices of the HVO, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I wish to ask my learned friend to be very precise when she says under whose authority she thinks the municipalities were. [In English] "Under the auspices of the HVO." What HVO, who?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let's look at P00303, and this may help us along. P00303. You actually have it in front of you on the screen as well, and if we could go to Articles 13, 14 and 15, second page of the English, second page of the B/C/S. There you go. I'm going to review these, and then we can talk about this. This is the 3rd of July, 1992, a statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority and administration in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.
